lead: Several forces act at one point: ropes on a ring, a bolt on a bracket, a hook carrying a load. Mechanics replaces them with one force doing the same job — the resultant. Forces are vectors, so their sizes do not add. Add the x parts to get R<sub>x</sub>, add the y parts to get R<sub>y</sub>, then rebuild one force. Every particle statics problem starts here.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.2 for vector addition, and Chapter 1.3 for resolving a force into components.

blocks.text: Put O at the meeting point. Take +x right, +y up. Measure θ anticlockwise from +x. A 40 N force straight down has θ = 270°.
F<sub>x</sub> = F cos θ,   F<sub>y</sub> = F sin θ
blocks.where: F is the force magnitude in newtons; θ is its angle in degrees anticlockwise from +x; F<sub>x</sub> and F<sub>y</sub> are the horizontal and vertical parts in newtons, each carrying its own sign.

blocks.text: Signs come from the calculator. cos 150° = −0.866 and sin 150° = +0.5, so 75 N at 150° gives −64.95 N and +37.5 N. Adding sizes, 60 + 100 + 75 + 40 = 275 N, is wrong.

R<sub>x</sub> = ΣF<sub>x</sub> = F<sub>1</sub>cos θ<sub>1</sub> + F<sub>2</sub>cos θ<sub>2</sub> + … ,   R<sub>y</sub> = ΣF<sub>y</sub> = F<sub>1</sub>sin θ<sub>1</sub> + F<sub>2</sub>sin θ<sub>2</sub> + …
blocks.where: R<sub>x</sub> and R<sub>y</sub> are the two totals in newtons; Σ means add over every force, one term per force.

items: Draw axes through O and fix the sign convention.
Convert every angle to θ anticlockwise from +x. Change slopes, bearings or angles from +y first.
Compute F cos θ and F sin θ, keeping calculator signs.
Add x parts to get R<sub>x</sub>; add y parts to get R<sub>y</sub>.

sections.h3: Rebuild one force from the two totals

blocks.text: R<sub>x</sub> and R<sub>y</sub> are perpendicular, so Pythagoras and tangent give size and direction.

blocks.where: R is the magnitude of the resultant in newtons; α is the acute angle in degrees between the resultant and the x-axis, always positive. If R<sub>x</sub> = 0, the resultant is vertical: θ = 90° when R<sub>y</sub> > 0, θ = 270° when R<sub>y</sub> < 0, and R = |R<sub>y</sub>|.

blocks.text: α alone is not the answer. tan⁻¹ returns a first-quadrant angle; place the resultant in its actual quadrant.
atan2(Ry, Rx) reads signs and returns the correct quadrant. On paper, use the table.

sections.h3: The force polygon checks the arithmetic

blocks.text: Draw forces tip to tail. Order is free because vector addition is commutative. Arrow from first tail to last tip is R.
The figure: 60 N along +x, 100 N at 60°, 75 N at 150°, 40 N down; closing arrow from O to E is 95.4 N.
If the last tip returns to the start, the polygon closes and R = 0. That is equilibrium; Chapter 1.6 turns it into equations.

items: A rough scale drawing catches a missing force or a 180° slip.
A closed sketch is not proof; confirm R<sub>x</sub> = 0 and R<sub>y</sub> = 0 to two decimal places.
Reversing order must give the same closing arrow.
Collinear: forces on one line add algebraically: 30 N right plus 20 N left is 10 N right.

Two forces F<sub>1</sub> and F<sub>2</sub> with angle γ between them: R = √(F<sub>1</sub>² + F<sub>2</sub>² + 2F<sub>1</sub>F<sub>2</sub>cos γ). At γ = 90° this is √(F<sub>1</sub>² + F<sub>2</sub>²); at γ = 180° it is |F<sub>1</sub> − F<sub>2</sub>|.
n equal forces F spaced 360°/n apart give R = 0. Three 100 N forces at 0°, 120°, 240° cancel exactly.
Usual wording: 'determine the resultant of the force system and its direction with the x-axis'. Magnitude and quadrant carry marks.
Some syllabi call this 'resultant of several concurrent forces in a plane'. Method is identical.

figure.caption: Four forces drawn tip to tail; the closing arrow from O to E is the resultant, 95.4 N at 61.8° from +x.

spec.aria: A force polygon drawn tip to tail with the four given forces; the single arrow from the start point O to the last tip E is the 95.4 N resultant.

examples.question: Four ropes pull on a ring at O. F<sub>1</sub> = 60 N at 0°, F<sub>2</sub> = 100 N at 60°, F<sub>3</sub> = 75 N at 150° and F<sub>4</sub> = 40 N at 270°, all angles measured anticlockwise from +x. Determine the resultant and its direction with the x-axis.
steps: Axes: +x right, +y up, θ anticlockwise. All forces act at O, so concurrent.
Direction: α = tan⁻¹(84.10 / 45.05) = tan⁻¹(1.867) = 61.8°. R<sub>x</sub> > 0 and R<sub>y</sub> > 0, so first quadrant and θ = α.
Rough visual check: the tip-to-tail sketch closes from O to E at about 95.4 N at 61.8°. The real check is R<sub>x</sub> = 45.05 N and R<sub>y</sub> = 84.10 N.
examples.answer: R = 95.4 N acting at 61.8° anticlockwise from +x, that is 61.8° above the horizontal to the right.
examples.check:
import math
F = [60, 100, 75, 40]
ang = [0, 60, 150, 270]
fx = sum(f * math.cos(math.radians(a)) for f, a in zip(F, ang))
fy = sum(f * math.sin(math.radians(a)) for f, a in zip(F, ang))
R = math.hypot(fx, fy)
theta = math.degrees(math.atan2(fy, fx))
print(round(fx, 1))
print(round(fy, 1))
print(round(R, 1))
print(round(theta, 1))

traps: Writing θ = tan⁻¹(R<sub>y</sub>/R<sub>x</sub>) when R<sub>x</sub> < 0. Use α = tan⁻¹(|R<sub>y</sub>|/|R<sub>x</sub>|), then place the resultant with the sign table: if R<sub>x</sub> < 0 and R<sub>y</sub> > 0, θ = 180° − α; if both are negative, θ = 180° + α; if R<sub>x</sub> > 0 and R<sub>y</sub> < 0, θ = 360° − α. Raw tan⁻¹(R<sub>y</sub>/R<sub>x</sub>) is 180° away only when R<sub>x</sub> < 0.
Adding magnitudes: 60 + 100 + 75 + 40 = 275 N. Valid only when all forces are collinear and in the same sense.
Angles from +y, from a wall, or as a slope 3 vertical to 4 horizontal: convert to θ anticlockwise from +x before cos or sin.
Calculator in radian mode: sin 60 gives −0.305 instead of 0.866.
Reporting R without quadrant, or saying '61.8° with the x-axis' when it points down and left. Direction needs magnitude and quadrant.

quiz.q: What is a coplanar concurrent force system?
quiz.a: Forces whose lines of action all lie in one plane and all pass through a single common point.

quiz.q: Write the two equations that give the components of the resultant.
quiz.a: R<sub>x</sub> = ΣF cos θ and R<sub>y</sub> = ΣF sin θ, with every θ measured anticlockwise from +x.

quiz.q: Why is 60 N + 100 N = 160 N a wrong statement for forces at 60° to each other?
quiz.a: Force is a vector. Magnitudes add only when parallel and in the same sense. At 60°, R = √(60² + 100² + 2 × 60 × 100 × cos 60°) = √19600 = 140 N.

quiz.q: Forces of 30 N along +x and 40 N along +y act at a point. Find the resultant and its direction.
quiz.a: R<sub>x</sub> = 30 N, R<sub>y</sub> = 40 N. R = √(900 + 1600) = 50 N. α = tan⁻¹(40/30) = 53.1°. First quadrant, so θ = 53.1° from +x.

quiz.q: Two forces of 50 N each act at a point with 120° between them. Find the resultant.
A system gives R<sub>x</sub> = −30 N and R<sub>y</sub> = −40 N. Find the resultant and explain what is wrong with the answer 53.1° from +x.
quiz.a: R = √(900 + 1600) = 50 N. α = tan⁻¹(40/30) = 53.1°. Both components are negative, so the resultant lies in the third quadrant: θ = 180° + 53.1° = 233.1°. Quoting 53.1° puts the force in the first quadrant, opposite to where it acts.

quiz.q: Three forces of 100 N act at a point at 0°, 120° and 240°. Without calculating components, argue that the resultant is zero, and state what the force polygon looks like.
quiz.a: The forces are equal and evenly spaced, so the arrangement repeats under a 120° rotation. A single non-zero resultant would rotate with it and also stay unchanged; only the zero vector can do that. Drawn tip to tail, the arrows form a closed equilateral triangle, so R = 0.

beyond: Not for the exam. Software uses atan2, which handles quadrants automatically. Robot sensors and physics engines sum force vectors this way many times per second. If the sum is not zero, the leftover vector accelerates the body; Unit 5 begins there. Search 'atan2' and 'vector sum of forces'.
